paper_title: SciGen-Verifier: A Multimodal Reasoner for Explainable Verification in Scientific Image Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In realistic education, a solution is often expressed not only in words but in a drawing--a circuit, a geometric construction, a function plot--and a teacher must grade the drawing as carefully as the text. Recent advances in unified multimodal models have enabled scientific image generation, yet verifying the correctness of these specialized visual outputs remains a critical bottleneck: errors often arise from intricate domain knowledge, structural reasoning, and multi-step instruction rather than surface-level artifacts. Existing verifiers mainly target natural images and compress judgement into scalar scores, leaving scientific coverage and explainable feedback for error correction underexplored. To bridge this gap, we make three main contributions. (1) We construct SciGen-Verify, a benchmark dedicated to explainable verification of scientific image generation, spanning instruction following, multidisciplinary reasoning, and world knowledge domains. It contains a three-tier hierarchical protocol over the binary judgement, supporting explanation, and corrective editing instruction. (2) We develop SciGen-Verifier, a reasoning-driven multimodal verifier trained via cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by a curriculum-based two-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. The rubric-guided process rewards first strengthen scientific reasoning exploration and outcome rewards subsequently align output with ground-truth annotation. (3) On SciGen-Verify, SciGen-Verifier achieves competitive performance against much larger proprietary models. It further serves as a practical online critic for iterative image rectification.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The field of multimodal models is undergoing remarkable revolution, with vision-language models (Hong et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026; Seed, 2026b) tackling complex visual reasoning and generative models (i.e., unified multimodal models (Deng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025b) and diffusion-based generators (Betker et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2024)) enabling high-fidelity visual synthesis. Recent advances in generative models are pushing text-to-image synthesis beyond opendomain natural scenes toward more specialized scientific image generation (Wang et al., 2025b; Ni et al., 2025). In educational scenarios, some scientific questions are answered by drawing rather than writing: sketching circuit, constructing geometric figure, or plotting function. As generative models begin to do homework in this visual form, natural question follows: who grades these drawings, and how? Unlike natural images, scientific images demand strict adherence to domain knowledge, structural reasoning, and multi-step instruction, where subtle deviations can cause the output to be scientifically invalid. Reliable verification of these specialized visual outputs thus emerges as critical bottleneck for trustworthy scientific image generation system. As illustrated in Fig. 1, errors in scientific image generation fundamentally differ from surficial artifacts in natural images: they manifest as violated physical or geometric constraints, missing critical Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Overview of SciGen-Verify benchmark across instruction following, multidisciplinary reasoning and world knowledge domains. The context image is the input image of the problem. components, and subtle misalignments with disciplinary facts. For instance, in physics reasoning scenario of Fig. 1, generative model tasked with drawing parallel circuit might mistakenly connect in series. Identifying such flaw goes far beyond pixel-level anomaly detection, which requires physical understanding to recognize the structural violation. Moreover, merely flagging these errors with binary judgement is insufficient for further correction (Chen et al., 2026; 2024). To effectively rectify scientific diagrams, verifier must explicitly articulate why the image is incorrect (e.g., pointing out the erroneous series connection) and prescribe exactly how to fix it (e.g., providing specific editing instructions). Thus, we refer to this triplet (i.e., binary judgement, explanation, and actionable editing instruction) as our explainable scientific image verification, which is overlooked by current multimodal verifiers. Despite recent progress in multimodal verification, two major limitations hinder its application to scientific image generation. First, prior verification benchmarks and reward models (Xu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026) are built for natural images, focusing on generic image-text alignment and human aesthetic preference. They neglect the scientific structural fidelity and domain-specific reasoning required for scientific image generation. Second, although recent benchmarks for scientific image generation (Wang et al., 2025b; Ni et al., 2025) introduce fine-grained evaluation rubrics, they serve merely as static and offline testbeds. Crucially, it still lacks dedicated verifier that can actively generate explainable and real-time feedback for scientific error correction, providing practical application for iterative image rectification. To bridge this gap, we aim to build benchmark and verifier model for explainable verification of scientific image generation. On the benchmark side, we construct SciGen-Verify, the first benchmark for this verification task, spanning three core domains (i.e., instruction following, multidisciplinary reasoning, and world knowledge) with hierarchical protocol over the binary judgement, explanation, and editing instruction. To ensure data quality, the benchmark is meticulously constructed through an AI-assisted annotation pipeline coupled with rigorous human expert inspection. On the model side, we develop SciGen-Verifier, an 8B multimodal verifier trained with cold-start supervised fine-tuning followed by curriculum-based two-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. It is motivated by the observation that SFT failures predominantly stem from incomplete evidence exploration. The first stage RL employs rubric-guided process reward to enforce comprehensive reasoning coverage, while the second stage uses an outcome reward to align the judgement, explanation and editing instruction with ground-truth annotation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (i) We construct SciGen-Verify, the first benchmark dedicated to the explainable verification of scientific image generation with hierarchical evaluation protocol. (ii) We train SciGen-Verifier-8B via curriculum-based two-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to strengthen scientific reasoning exploration and align corrective annotation. (iii) Empirical results demonstrate that our SciGen-Verifier matches much larger proprietary baselines, and serves as an online critic to progressively rectify errors during iterative test-time scaling.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multimodal Verification. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) stem from evolving reasoning paradigms (Liu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025b) and unified generative capabilities (Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a). To evaluate multimodal understanding, Li et al. (2025c) propose testbed for multimodal preference alignment. VisualPRM (Wang et al., 2025a) extends to step-wise process verification on reasoning trace. Meanwhile, the emergence of generative models has spurred efforts to develop automatic verification for text-to-image tasks. To overcome the coarse semantic similarity of early metrics like CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021), ProImage-Bench (Ni et al., 2025) probes fine-grained semantic alignment via question-answer pairs. Beyond static scoring, explainable feedback generation has been explored for multimodal reasoning errors, from distractor correction in visual commonsense reasoning (Chen et al., 2024) to educational diagnostic reasoning with error tracing and correction (Chen et al., 2026), whereas scientific image generation still lacks dedicated verifier that articulates why an image fails and how to fix it. Scientific Image Generation. Most generative models are confined to open-domain natural scenes and struggle to satisfy scientific image generation demands. To bridge this gap, emerging works explore domain-specific generation via code rendering (Qiao et al., 2025; Belouadi et al., 2025) or direct visual synthesis (Zhu et al., 2026), and SciIR (Ma et al., 2026) further provides large-scale training dataset and benchmark for scientific image generation. For evaluation, some multidisciplinary benchmarks (e.g., MMMG (Luo et al., 2026), SridBench (Chang et al., 2025) and ScImage (Zhang et al., 2025a)) rely on holistic metrics. While recent frameworks (e.g., GenExam (Wang et al., 2025b), ProImage-Bench (Ni et al., 2025)) advance to structural rubrics for fine-grained evaluation, they merely serve as static testbeds without explainable error correction. 3 SciGen-Verify BENCHMARK

sections.title: 3.1 BENCHMARK OVERVIEW
sections.content: To systematically assess the verification of scientific visual outcomes, we introduce SciGen-Verify, comprehensive benchmark with three core domains: (i) Instruction Following tests the MLLMs adherence to multi-step constraints for synthesizing or editing scientific images; (ii) Multidisciplinary Reasoning probes logical and structural fidelity in complex STEM diagrams (e.g., figures strictly governed by physical or geometric laws); and (iii) World Knowledge assesses reliance on domainspecific factual fidelity. Moving beyond generic holistic evaluation, SciGen-Verify formulates this verification as an executable reasoning task. Specifically, each sample is annotated with binary correctness judgement, with detailed explanation. Crucially, for anomalous outputs (i.e., false judgement), the MLLM is required to generate actionable editing instructions for error correction, offering pathway for image rectification. In the following, we describe the construction process of SciGen-Verify, as shown in Fig. 2. More details are provided in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3.2 DATA SOURCE
sections.content: To ensure our benchmark covers real-world scientific image generation scenarios, we collect highquality data samples spanning three core domains: Instruction Following, Multidisciplinary Reasoning, and World Knowledge. Since these sources vary in format and annotation granularity, we perform different preprocessing methods to standardize them for further unified verification. Instruction Following. This domain requires the verifier to accurately assess adherence to complex, multi-step textual constraints for diagram synthesis and modification (e.g., Draw coordinate plane, plot the points A(1, 2) and B(4, 2), and add the line segment AB with its midpoint labeled M. . . ). We collect data from V-Interaction (Qiao et al., 2025) and MathCanvas (Shi et al., 2025) datasets. Specifically, MathCanvas directly provides images and potential textual instruction pairs for image generation and editing tasks. V-Interaction consists of interleaved reasoning trajectories where intermediate visual images are updated via code. While it provides the before and after code-rendered images for each reasoning step, it lacks explicit natural language editing instruction. Hence, we prompt Claude-Sonnet-5 (Anthropic, 2026b) to analyze the code differences between adjacent visual images and generate the corresponding natural language editing instructions. 3 Figure 2: Construction workflow of our SciGen-Verify benchmark, including data collection, negative sample construction, and annotation with expert review. Multidisciplinary Reasoning. Beyond explicit instruction following, this domain evaluates whether verifiers can assess scientific diagrams that serve as answers to discipline-specific reasoning problems. It requires verifier to interpret subject-specific problems and infer the expected diagrammatic solution, such as circuit connections, chemical structures, function plots. To construct this subset, we aggregate data from three primary streams. First, we collect scientific diagrams from CoSyn (Yang et al., 2025b) and DaTikZ-V3 (Belouadi et al., 2024), which contain code-rendered figures across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and other STEM subjects. For each sample, we prompt Claude-Opus-4.8 (Anthropic, 2026a) to inspect the corresponding code and synthesize reasoning-intensive problem statements, for which the original figure serves as the ground-truth answer. Second, we adapt multiplechoice questions from EMMA (Hao et al., 2025) by selecting samples whose options are unique images. We then reformulate them into scientific image generation tasks, where correct options serve as reference images. Finally, we crawl educational examination papers and extract authentic diagram-construction problems, e.g., drawing circuit according to component constraints. World Knowledge. Beyond explicit instruction following and multidisciplinary reasoning, this domain evaluates whether the verifier ensures the visual content faithfully aligns with established scientific concepts (e.g., illustrating the stratigraphic layers of the Earths mantle). First, we systematically mine Wikipedia with curated discipline-specific taxonomy tags and keywords. Then, we crawl wide spectrum of professional scientific images. Second, we choose images from AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016), which features diverse pedagogical visualizations, including ecological food webs, microscopic cellular anatomies, and macroscopic geophysical processes. Since both sources provide visual assets without textual descriptions, we employ Gemini-3-Flash (Google, 2025) to generate concept-centric captions capturing scientific entities and relations as problem statements.

sections.title: 3.3 BENCHMARK CURATION PIPELINE
sections.content: We construct SciGen-Verify through systematical curation pipeline to ensure both comprehensive disciplinary coverage and annotation reliability. Based on the collected data sources, we sample subset according to their disciplinary taxonomies. We construct corresponding negative samples via controlled perturbations. To support explainable verification, we finally utilize AI-assisted annotation followed by rigorous expert review to equip these samples with reliable judgement and detailed explanation and potential editing instruction.

sections.title: 3.3.1 NEGATIVE SAMPLE CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: To evaluate the verifiers robustness against genuine scientific mistakes rather than trivial mismatches, we must ensure the constructed negative samples are highly challenging and realistic. Inspired by (Zhang et al., 2025b), we design the following two automated strategies to construct negative samples. Visual Perturbation. We construct negative data by modifying the visual output while keeping the original problem statements fixed. Depending on the image format, we process them as follows: For samples equipped with rendering code, we prompt Claude-Sonnet-5 to identify error-prone elements within the scientific context and subtly modify the code to render an incorrect diagram (e.g., bypassing resistor). For other reference images, inspired by (Yang et al., 2025a), we employ Gemini-3-Pro to simulate an experienced teacher. By analyzing the input problem statement and reference image, the model identifies tricky knowledge points and common student misconceptions, subsequently outputting corresponding editing instruction. We then feed this instruction and the original image into Qwen-Image-Edit (Wu et al., 2025a) to generate rigorously flawed candidate image. Furthermore, to mitigate unintended artifacts introduced by the generative model, we introduce an automated filtering stage with Gemini-3-Flash. Before any human review, it scans the generated candidate images to discard low-quality samplesspecifically targeting severe blurriness, illegible text, or clear failures against the editing instruction. This ensures the visual errors reflect authentic human student cognitive mistakes rather than poor generation fidelity. Textual Perturbation. Alternatively, we construct negative data by altering the textual problem statements while retaining the original correct candidate image. We utilize Gemini-3-Pro to deeply inspect the critical solving steps and generative requirements of the original problem. Specifically, the model first extracts key scientific entities, quantitative parameters, and structural relationships from the prompt. It then systematically injects counterfactual conditions by altering specific details, such as reversing structural logic (e.g., changing required parallel circuit connection to series), modifying numerical values (e.g., altering specified geometric angle), or substituting domainspecific attributes (e.g., replacing required chemical functional group). This strategy creates logical counterfactual mismatch between the text and candidate image.

sections.title: 3.3.2 ANNOTATION AND EXPERT REVIEW
sections.content: AI-Assisted Initial Annotation. We first utilize Gemini-3.1-Pro to generate comprehensive initial annotations. Specifically, for the binary judgement, the model is prompted to output step-bystep reasoning rationale as explanation. For negative samples, it also synthesizes precise editing instruction designed to rectify the identified visual errors in the false image. Expert Review and Refinement. To ensure the benchmarks rigor, we recruit 10 domain experts comprising two graduate students for each of the five target disciplines (Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, and Geography)to conduct comprehensive human evaluation. To prevent prior cognitive bias, paired positive and negative samples are partitioned into two separate groups. Each sample is independently reviewed by domain-matched experts, and it is retained only if both experts explicitly approve its correctness and necessary refinements. The process is structured around two core stages: (i) Multi-Dimensional Quality Filter. The experts evaluate the samples based on three strict criteria: Visual Fidelity, filtering out generated images with severe blurriness or rendering artifacts; Task Difficulty, discarding overly simplistic cases that lack reasoning depth; and Annotation Correctness, verifying the strict factual accuracy of the binary judgements, reasoning rationales, and editing instructions. (ii) Manual Refinement and Verification. Samples with unresolvable ambiguities or fatal visual errors are directly discarded. For minor textual flaws (e.g., slight hallucinations or vague instructions), the first expert from the corresponding discipline manually rewrites the text to ensure the rationales are logical and the editing instructions are actionable. Subsequently, the second expert independently reviews these modifications. The sample is retained only if the second expert approves the refined results. Ultimately, this rigorous process yields the finalized SciGen-Verify benchmark, comprising 1,350 data samples: 406 for instruction following, 287 for multidisciplinary reasoning, and 657 for world knowledge.

sections.title: 3.4 EVALUATION METHODS
sections.content: We evaluate verifiers using strict three-tier hierarchical protocol. Detailed formulations are provided in Appendix A.3. We design three cascading metrics: judgement (Acca), explanation (Acce), and editing instruction Accuracy (Acci). Specifically, Acca is rule-based metric that solely measures binary prediction correctness, whereas Acce and Acci are model-based metrics evaluated by proprietary LLMs to assess logical consistency and actionable correction. Both judges are validated against three human experts on 300 sampled instances, where the judgehuman agreement (κ 0.76) approaches the humanhuman ceiling (κ = 0.83), and the evaluation is further shown to be robust to the choice of judge (Appendix A.4).

sections.title: 4 SCIGEN-VERIFIER MODEL
sections.content: The inherent complexity of scientific image verification motivates us to investigate methods that can progressively strengthen the capabilities of current advanced MLLMs. We therefore develop the reasoning-augmented SciGen-Verifier through two-stage training pipeline: supervised finetuning (SFT) cold start (Sec. 4.1) that endows the model with structured reasoning output and basic verification ability, followed by curriculum-based reinforcement learning (RL) phase (Sec. 4.2) with progressive reward signals to further strengthen its reasoning depth and output reliability. The overall pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 5 (Appendix C.1).

sections.title: 4.1 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING
sections.content: SFT Data Construction. The SFT corpus is drawn from the same upstream sources as SciGenVerify (Sec. 3), and the two are split at the source-sample level so that source problem or image, together with all of its perturbed variants, belongs to exactly one set, ensuring strictly no data overlap (see Appendix C.1). To efficiently scale annotations, we utilize Seed-2.0-Pro (Seed, 2026b) to generate structured responses strictly following an XML-style template: <think> reasoning trace </think> <answer> binary judgement </answer> <explanation> rationale </explanation> <edit> editing instruction for false instances </edit>. To guarantee quality, we apply rejection sampling (Guo et al., 2025a) to retain only instances where the binary judgement matches the ground truth and the explanation is validated by Gemini-3-Flash. It finally yields 48,311 training instances. Training. We instantiate SciGen-Verifier from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) and perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on the curated corpus DSFT. We optimize the model πθ via the standard next-token prediction objective: LSFT(θ) = E(x,y)DSFT [log πθ(y x)] , where denotes the problem statement with potential input images and denotes the curated tagged response. This stage transfers structured reasoning and subject-specific verification knowledge into the verifier, which is reliable initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. (1)

sections.title: 4.2 REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
sections.content: After SFT, SciGen-Verifier acquires basic verification ability and outputs with structured format. However, its judgement remains unreliable on hard instances since the reasoning trace often lacks subject-specific evidence. Toward this end, we adopt GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to perform curriculum-based reinforcement learning pipeline: the first stage sharpens the verifiers judgement through rubric-guided reward, while the second stage directly refines its judgement, explanations, and editing instructions through an outcome reward. We use the SFT model to perform = 8 rollout sampling across the SFT corpus and unseen complementary data. Inspired by (An et al., 2025), we evaluate the binary judgements using rule-based metrics and retain 15K queries that yield partial success (i.e., {1, . . . , 7} correct rollouts) to provide appropriate challenging data for RL.

sections.title: 4.2.2 RL WITH RUBRIC-GUIDED REWARD
sections.content: Rewarding CoT with Rubrics. To supervise the reasoning process rather than solely the final judgement, our first-stage reward evaluates whether the generated reasoning trace explicitly mentions checkpoints defined in an instance-specific scientific rubric (e.g., Is the curve passing through the origin?). These rubrics are produced by dedicated rubric generator, which is trained on data from the same upstream sources. Following (Zhang et al., 2026), we also rigorously validate the rubric generator on test data  (Table 6)  , proving its reliability (see Appendix B.3). For each rollout τ produced by the verifier policy πθ, coverage checker πϕ assesses whether each checkpoint rj is correctly addressed within τ reasoning trace, yielding binary indicator cj(τ ) {0, 1}. The rubric-guided reward is then defined as the coverage ratio over the checkpoints within rubrics: Rrubric(τ ) = 1 (cid:88) j=1 cj(τ ). (2) Total Reward. We simultaneously introduce binary judgement reward Rjudge. To balance processlevel exploration and correctness optimization, the first-stage reward combines the judgement and rubric signals via dynamic coefficients: R1(τ ) = αtRjudge(τ ) + βtRrubric(τ ). sections.title: 5.1 PERFORMANCE COMPARISON
sections.content: Table 1 reports the evaluation results on SciGen-Verify benchmark. We have the following findings: (i) Frontier MLLMs still exhibit limited scientific image verification capability. Despite their established multimodal reasoning prowess, leading proprietary MLLMs remain far from reliable on SciGen-Verify. Even the strongest baseline Qwen3.8-Max (86.03% overall Acca) and frontier flagships such as Gemini-3.5-Flash and GPT-6-Astra suffer precipitous drop once the protocol demands explainable feedback: GPT-6-Astra falls from 75.71% overall Acca to 53.59% Acci, and Gemini-3.5-Flash from 81.38% to 56.54%, revealing profound deficiency in fine-grained mistake localization and correction. More notably, OmniVerifier-7B, model trained for evaluating generic images, performs poorly on SciGen-Verify. This stark contrast demonstrates that scientific verification extends far beyond generic text-image alignment and demands intricate disciplinary knowledge. (ii) SciGen-Verifier achieves robust verification performance. Built upon lightweight 8B backbone, SciGen-Verifier demonstrates robust generalization across all three core evaluation domains. It achieves the highest overall Acca of 86.28%, outperforming the strongest baseline Qwen3.8-Max (86.03%) as well as frontier proprietary models such as Gemini-3.5-Flash (+4.90%) and GPT-6-Astra (+10.57%). Notably, our model exhibits exceptional proficiency in world knowledge verification, establishing new state-of-the-art with 94.21% Acca, 91.53% Acce, and 65.48% Acci, which eclipses Qwen3.8-Max by +6.45%, +4.41%, and +5.67%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that our curriculum-based reinforcement learning effectively endows the SFT model with profound scientific deliberation capabilities. (iii) Correcting scientific errors is significantly harder than identifying them. As observed in Table 1, there is sharp performance drop for all models on the Acci metric. While current MLLMs can successfully diagnose scientific inconsistencies, they struggle to prescribe precise modifications. For instance, Gemini-3.5-Flash and GPT-6-Astra are capped at 56.54% and 53.59% overall Acci, respectively, and even the strongest baseline Qwen3.8-Max attains only 64.75%. Similarly, despite its strong diagnostic capability, our SciGen-Verifier-8B obtains 57.42%. This performance gap highlights that synthesizing actionable corrective edits remains major bottleneck in scientific image verification. Overcoming this limitation is crucial to rectify flawed scientific images generated by generative models. 8 Figure 4: Case study. (a) Comparison with strong baseline. sections.title: 5.2 EFFECT OF EXPLICIT REASONING
sections.content: To evaluate the impact of explicit reasoning, we compare models trained with and without chain-of-thought (CoT) across both SFT and RL stages  (Fig. 3)  . Directly predicting outcomes (w/o CoT SFT) yields competitive Acca of 81.0% yet suffers severe performance collapse when articulating faithful feedback (Acce: 65.9%; Acci: 36.4%). Applying RL to this direct-prediction paradigm (w/o CoT SFT+RL)1 brings negligible gains, revealing that RL fundamentally struggles to optimize complex visual editing without intermediate logical grounding. Conversely, integrating CoT (w/ CoT SFT) effectively mitigates this degradation, lifting Acce and Acci to 75.3% and 46.7% with marginal Acca concession. Most crucially, the synergy between CoT and RL (w/ CoT SFT+RL) maximizes the models potential, propelling overall Acca to 86.3% and Acci to 57.4%, with the most pronounced gains observed in the instruction-following domain. These results firmly establish that intermediate CoT steps are not merely optional features, but essential structural prerequisites enabling RL to synthesize reliable corrections in scientific verification. Figure 3: Effect of CoT reasoning.

sections.title: 5.3 EFFECT OF CURRICULUM-BASED RL TRAINING
sections.content: To validate the efficacy of our two-stage curriculum RL, we analyze the performance of SciGenVerifier across different training strategies  (Table 2)  . While supervised fine-tuning (S) establishes foundational capabilities, directly applying outcome-level rewards without process-level grounding (S + R2) yields suboptimal improvements, prematurely capping reasoning Acca at 84.9% and Acci at 51.2%. This highlights critical risk of premature convergence in RL: without explicitly encouraging initial exploration within reasoning traces, the model exploits shortcuts and settles into local optima. Our decoupled curriculum effectively circumvents this limitation. Stage 1 RL, governed by rubric rewards, enforces rigorous visual evidence exploration, pushing reasoning Acca to 86.1%. Building upon this expanded reasoning capacity, Stage 2 introduces outcome-level alignment to teach precise articulation. This synergy successfully unlocks the models true upper bound, propelling overall Acca to 86.3% and Acci to 57.4%, confirming that initial rubric-guided exploration is an indispensable prerequisite for maximizing the potential of scientific image verification. 1The prompt requires the model to emit the fixed format without <think> field and rubric-guided reward.

sections.content: As shown in Fig. 4 (a), while Seed-2.0-Pro exhibits false-positive hallucination by overlooking the explicitly requested dotted lines, our model precisely localizes this subtle visual violation and formulates actionable editing instructions. Beyond benchmark performance, Fig. 4 (b) illustrates the deployment of SciGen-Verifier as an online critic for image rectification with iterative test-time scaling (TTS) (Appendix D.2). By iteratively diagnosing geometric mislabeling and mathematical inconsistencies, our model provides precise critiques that guide the generative model to self-correct.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: This paper focuses on explainable verification for scientific image generation. We first construct SciGen-Verify benchmark for this verification task, covering three representative domains. Second, we develop SciGen-Verifier through curriculum-based two-stage reinforcement learning pipeline, where rubric-guided process rewards strengthen reasoning exploration and outcome rewards explicitly align with ground truth. Extensive experiments confirm that explicit reasoning and curriculum-based reinforcement learning are jointly indispensable, and show that SciGen-Verifier serves as an online critic for iterative image rectification.

For positive examples, the annotation explains why the candidate image satisfies the scientific image generation or editing instruction by explicitly mapping visual evidence to textual constraints. For negative examples, the annotation identifies the violated scientific facts, structural relations, or instruction-following requirements, and then provides an actionable editing instruction for correcting the image. AI-Assisted Annotation. We use MLLM-based annotation to generate initial explanations and editing instructions with the prompt templates in Appendix E.1. The annotation model is instructed to inspect the problem statement and candidate image jointly, and to ground its explanation in concrete visual evidence rather than generic comments. For false examples, the generated editing instruction must describe localized and executable changes that would make the image consistent with the original instruction. Human Verification. Following the review protocol in Sec. 3, every sample is independently reviewed by two domain-matched experts, who check the binary judgement, explanation, and editing instruction. Samples with unresolvable ambiguities, severe rendering failures, or unsupported scientific claims are discarded. For minor textual defects, the first expert rewrites the explanation or editing instruction, and the sample is retained only after the second expert approves the refined result. We then compute the hierarchical metrics in Appendix A.3, where explanation and editing-instruction quality are evaluated with the judge prompts in Appendix E.3. B.1.1 RUBRIC CONSTRUCTION PIPELINE We design highly automated pipeline to translate complex scientific generation requirements into structured, quantifiable rubrics. Given problem statement and its associated reference image, the pipeline proceeds through four successive stages. Multimodal Constraint Extraction. We leverage Doubao-Seed-2.0-Lite (Seed, 2026b) to jointly parse the textual problem statement and reference image, extracting core scientific indicators that govern the figures correctness. These indicators are formulated as high-level evaluation criteria. Atomic Point Expansion. Each criterion is further decomposed into set of fine-grained checking points, where each point is formulated as an objective binary question (Yes/No). This decomposition reduces macroscopic quality judgements into atomic, unit-test-like verification signals, effectively mitigating subjective evaluation bias. Weighted Score Allocation. The total score for each rubric is strictly capped at 10.0. Weights are dynamically allocated across criteria based on the structural complexity and the risk of visual failure, ensuring that scientifically critical aspects receive proportional emphasis. Quality Refinement and Denoising. We conduct manual filtering combined with automated sanity checks to discard sub-optimal annotations, ensuring high interpretability and scientific consistency across the dataset. (ii) Frontier MLLMs exhibit clear coverageprecision trade-off. Across baseline models, we observe systematic tension between coverage and conservativeness. For example, Qwen3.5-397B obtains the highest Knowledge-domain NHR (80.99), suggesting fewer hallucinated checking points, yet its substantially lower RR (48.26) indicates that it misses large portion of expert-annotated rules. Conversely, smaller models such as Qwen3.5-9B achieve moderate RR but suffer from severe hallucination (51.03 overall NHR). In contrast, the trained rubric generator maintains both high coverage and high non-hallucination rate simultaneously, yielding the strongest SF1 in all three domains. (iii) These results justify using the rubric generators outputs as process-level supervision for SciGen-Verifier, as the generated rubrics faithfully recover the majority of expertannotated rules while introducing minimal hallucinated constraints.

sections.title: C MORE EXPERIMENT DETAILS
sections.content: C.1 TRAINING DETAILS OF SCIGEN-VERIFIER Overall Pipeline. Figure 5 summarizes the complete training pipeline. Given problem statement and candidate image, the verifier policy πθ, initialized from the cold-start SFT checkpoint, samples group of rollouts that follow the tagged output format described below. The first RL stage attaches two auxiliary components to these rollouts: the rubric generator, which produces instance-specific checkpoints r1, . . . , rn (Appendix B), and coverage checker πϕ, which marks the checkpoints explicitly addressed in the <think> trace and thereby yields the coverage ratio Rrubric. This processlevel signal is blended with the rule-based judgement reward Rjudge under the mastery-driven schedule (αt, βt) detailed in Appendix C.1.1. The second RL stage drops the rubric branch and instead scores the <explanation> and <edit> fields against ground-truth annotations with LLM judges, producing Rexp-edit, while Rjudge is retained to protect judgement accuracy. Both stages optimize πθ with GRPO; only the reward composition changes between them. Output Format. SciGen-Verifier follows the same tripartite interface used in SciGen-Verify: given scientific image generation or editing instruction and its candidate image, it outputs binary judgement, supporting explanation, and an optional editing instruction. During both SFT and RL, responses are constrained to an XML-style template consisting of <think>, <answer>, <explanation>, and <edit> fields. The <think> field contains the intermediate reasoning trace, while the latter three fields provide the structured outputs used for parsing and evaluation. For benchmark inference and baseline evaluation, we use the verifier prompt shown in Appendix E.2. Cold-start SFT. We initialize SciGen-Verifier from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) and perform full-parameter SFT for two epochs on the curated 48,311-instance corpus described in Sec. 4.1. The corpus is approximately balanced between true and false instances and contains 19,678 instruction-following, 20,367 multidisciplinary-reasoning, and 8,266 world-knowledge examples. To mitigate data imbalance across categories, we apply data-level temperature sampling during SFT, where the sampling quota of each subset is proportional to qi n1/T with = 1.5. The resulting SFT checkpoint serves as the initialization for all subsequent GRPO stages. TrainTest Separation. Although the SFT corpus and SciGen-Verify share upstream sources, they are split at the source-sample level rather than the instance level: all instances derived from the same source problem or image, including its perturbed positive and negative variants produced by the visual and textual perturbation strategies in Sec. 3, are assigned to exactly one of the two sets. Consequently, neither benchmark sample nor any of its variants can flow into the training data, and Figure 5: Overview of the SciGen-Verifier training pipeline. Starting from the cold-start SFT checkpoint, the verifier policy πθ samples rollouts τ1, . . . , τN (N =K=8) for each problem statement and candidate image, each consisting of <think> trace, binary answer, and an explanation with an editing instruction. In Stage 1, the rubric generator produces instance-specific checkpoints r1, . . . , rn, coverage checker πϕ measures how many of them are addressed in the reasoning trace (Rrubric), and this process reward is blended with the rule-based judgement reward Rjudge through the mastery-driven coefficients αt and βt (Eq. 3). In Stage 2, Rjudge is combined with the LLM-judged explanation-editing reward Rexp-edit (Eq. 4). Both stages update πθ with GRPO. the split is mutually exclusive by construction. The same rule is applied to the RL query pool and the SciGen-Rubric training split. Stage 1 RL. For the first RL stage, we use the SFT model to perform = 8 rollouts for each candidate query and retain 15K partially successful queries whose binary judgements are correct in {1, . . . , 7} rollouts. This selection removes trivial samples that are already solved in all rollouts while preserving instances that still expose meaningful reward variation. The policy is optimized with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) using the rubric-guided reward in Eq. 3, which combines judgement correctness and rubric coverage through dynamic coefficients. This stage primarily strengthens evidence exploration and scientific constraint coverage in the generated <think> traces. Stage 2 RL. The second RL stage further polishes the structured outputs using 685 fully annotated examples with answer, explanation, and editing-instruction supervision. Unlike Stage 1, which emphasizes process-level exploration, this stage directly optimizes the semantic alignment of the final explanation and editing instruction through the outcome reward in Eq. 4. To avoid degrading the judgement ability learned in the first stage, answer correctness remains part of the reward throughout this stage. This two-stage design first establishes robust scientific verification and then improves the actionable feedback required by SciGen-Verify evaluation. Training Infrastructure. All SFT and RL experiments are implemented based on fork of ms-swift, with additional support for data-level temperature sampling and difficulty-aware GRPO sampling. In SFT, temperature sampling with = 1.5 rebalances category exposure across instruction following, multidisciplinary reasoning, and world knowledge. In RL, the sampler first expands the candidate prompt pool for rollout generation and then selects prompt groups with higher intra-group reward variance for optimization. This mechanism is independent of the reward definition and improves the density of informative GRPO updates. C.1.1 DETAILS OF RUBRIC-GUIDED REWARD We provide additional details on the dynamic weighting strategy used in Eq. 3. The central challenge in combining judgement supervision and rubric-guided process supervision lies in their asymmetric 19 reliability. While judgement correctness directly reflects the verifiers optimization objective, rubric coverage provides only proxy signal for reasoning quality and may occasionally reward partially relevant or incomplete reasoning traces. To preserve this asymmetry, we treat judgement correctness as the dominant optimization signal and use rubric coverage primarily as an auxiliary shaping reward. Specifically, the first-stage reward is formulated as: R1(τ ) = αtRjudge(τ ) + βtRrubric(τ ), (12) where αt and βt dynamically control the relative contribution of judgement correctness and rubric coverage throughout training. To adaptively balance exploration and optimization, we estimate the training mastery using moving average of recent judgement accuracy: mt [0, 1], (13) where larger values indicate stronger verifier performance. Based on the estimated mastery, the weighting coefficients are scheduled as: αt = αmaxmρ , βt = βmax(1 mt)ρ, (15) where αmax and βmax denote the maximum weighting coefficients and ρ > 0 controls the sharpness of the curriculum schedule. To ensure that judgement correctness remains the principal optimization target, we further impose: (14) αmax > βmax, (16) which prevents the auxiliary rubric-guided reward from dominating the optimization objective. This adaptive weighting induces curriculum-like transition during reinforcement learning. In early training, when judgement accuracy remains low (small mt), rubric-guided supervision receives relatively larger weight, encouraging the verifier to explore relevant scientific checkpoints, visual evidence, and disciplinary constraints. As training progresses and verifier accuracy improves, optimization gradually shifts toward judgement correctness, allowing the policy to refine decision-making while retaining process-level guidance. Conceptually, this formulation can be interpreted as soft relaxation of outcome-gated process supervision. Rather than explicitly suppressing process rewards for incorrect predictions, the verifier progressively shifts from exploration-oriented reasoning supervision toward judgement-centric optimization as policy competence improves. We found this simpler adaptive formulation to be empirically more stable while preserving the intended asymmetry between process-level supervision and outcome correctness. C.2 BASELINES IMPLEMENTATION We compare SciGen-Verifier against 15 leading MLLMs, including proprietary models GPT-6-Astra, Gemini-3-Flash, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Gemini-3.5-Flash (Google, 2025), Seed1.8(Seed, 2026a), Seed-2.0-Pro (Seed, 2026b), MiMo-V2-Omni (Li et al., 2025b), Qwen3.8-Max, GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash; open-source models Qwen3.5-397B (Alibaba Cloud Community, 2026), Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, and Qwen3-VL-235B-Thinking (Bai et al., 2025), as well as OmniVerifier-7B (Zhang et al., 2025b), multimodal verifier designed for visual verification. Table 7 shows their details. To ensure fair comparison, all baseline MLLMs are evaluated under the same input-output protocol as SciGen-Verifier. Given the problem statement and candidate image, each model is instructed with the verifier prompt in Appendix E.2 to make binary judgement and provide an explanation; when the predicted answer is false, it is additionally required to generate an editing instruction. We keep the prompt template consistent across proprietary APIs, open-source MLLMs, and the OmniVerifier-7B baseline, except for minor formatting wrappers required by different inference interfaces. Decoding and Parsing. For each model, we parse the final response into answer, explanation, and edit fields. If the model does not strictly follow the XML-style template, we apply conservative rule-based parser to extract the first unambiguous binary judgement and the corresponding free-form rationale. Responses without valid binary judgement are treated as incorrect for Acca, and their explanation and editing-instruction scores are consequently set to zero by the cascading protocol. For positive samples, the <edit> field is not used in evaluation; for negative samples, missing or non-actionable editing instruction is scored by the editing-instruction judge as invalid. 20 Table 7: The details of the baseline models in our comparison. sections.title: D MORE EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS
sections.content: D.1 EXPLORATION OF REINFORCEMENT LEARNING We further analyze how reinforcement learning contributes to SciGen-Verifier and rubric generator. For SciGen-Verifier, the central issue is how to expose the model to queries that are sufficiently challenging and how to prevent auxiliary rubric coverage from overwhelming judgement correctness. For rubric generator, the key question is whether verifier feedback can provide meaningful signal for improving the discriminability of generated checking points. D.1.1 RL DATA SELECTION FOR SCIGEN-VERIFIER. Following Sec. 4.2, we sample each candidate query = 8 times with the SFT verifier and compute the number of correct binary judgements. Consistently correct queries offer limited learning signal due to minimal reward diversity, while consistently incorrect queries often induce noisy supervision with weak preference contrast. We therefore retain partially successful queries, namely those with {1, . . . , 7} correct rollouts, and construct 15K-query RL pool. This selection makes each GRPO group more likely to contain both successful and failed responses, thereby improving reward contrast during policy optimization. 21 Figure 6: Sequential TTS case demonstrations with SciGen-Verifier feedback. D.1.2 STAGE-WISE RL FOR SCIGEN-VERIFIER. As shown in Table 2, SFT alone establishes basic verification ability but remains insufficient for generating faithful corrections. Stage 1 RL improves the reasoning and judgement metrics by rewarding explicit coverage of rubric checkpoints in the <think> trace. However, because this stage mainly supervises evidence exploration, its improvement on editing instruction accuracy remains limited. Stage 2 RL directly adds outcome-level supervision for explanation and editing instruction, leading to the strongest overall performance. These results support the curriculum design: reliable scientific verification should first be strengthened through process-level exploration and then aligned with textual feedback quality. D.1.3 RL WITH SCIGEN-VERIFIER FEEDBACK. During GRPO, we employ SciGen-Verifier as the reward source for training rubric generator. The Verifiers principal capability is to judge whether an image satisfies given instruction, and each binary checking point emitted by rubric generator is itself an image-verification instruction. Pointwise evaluation therefore directly reuses the judgement capability already acquired by the Verifier. Feeding the entire rubric = {(ck, Pk, wk)}K k=1 in single query would push the input off the Verifiers training distribution; we therefore adopt point-wise verification protocol that pairs each checking point pk,j Pk individually with the candidate image and queries the Verifier for its satisfaction status. For each training instance, we construct one positive imageinstruction pair that satisfies the underlying scientific constraints and one contrastive negative pair constructed from the corresponding training data. The negative pair uses the same visual asset with modified instruction, making the image valid for the positive pair but invalid for the negative pair. rubric generator first emits R, after which the Verifier evaluates every point pk,j against each pair under the point-wise protocol. Let zk,j(V ) {0, 1} denote the Verifiers binary result for checking point pk,j on image , where zk,j(V ) = 1 indicates that the point is satisfied. The criterion-level score is computed as ϕk(V, R) = 1 nk nk(cid:88) j=1 zk,j(V ), where nk = Pk. The image-level score is then aggregated by criterion weights: S(V, R) = (cid:88) k=1 wk ϕk(V, R), (17) (18) where (cid:80)K contrastive instance. The reward decomposes into discriminability term and format term, k=1 wk = 10.0. This produces positive score S+ and negative score for the paired = λs Rscore + Rfmt, (19) with the score reward defined piecewise as S+ 7.0, Rscore = , S+ > 7.0. 1.0, S+ 10.0 The positive-score threshold guards the basic faithfulness of R: if the positive pair cannot exceed 7.0, the rubric has failed to capture the constraints that the valid image necessarily satisfies and is treated as structurally invalid, receiving fixed negative reward. Above the threshold, the margin S+ governs the reward and directly quantifies discriminabilitya wider margin indicates that the checking points sharply localize the distinguishing features between the positive and negative pairs, whereas vanishing margin reflects rubric that no longer separates the two and is penalized accordingly. The format term Rfmt enforces structural validity of the emitted rubric: the response must be valid JSON encoding = {(ck, Pk, wk)}K k=1, where each element carries weight wk subject to (cid:80)K k=1 wk = 10. Full compliance yields 1.0; any violation yields 0.0. (20) D.2 APPLICATION OF TEST-TIME SCALING Beyond offline verification, SciGen-Verifier can be used as an online critic for iterative test-time scaling (TTS) of scientific image generation. Given an original generation prompt, we first obtain an initial image from Wan2.6-t2i (Alibaba Cloud Community, 2025) and query SciGen-Verifier with the verifier prompt in Appendix E.2. If the verifier predicts true, the procedure stops early and returns the current image. If the verifier predicts false, the system decides between regeneration and local editing based on the predicted editing instruction: editing instructions containing three or more correction items or global-regeneration keywords trigger regeneration, while localized corrections are sent to Wan2.6-image (Alibaba Cloud Community, 2025) for image editing. The edited or regenerated image is then passed back to the verifier, and the process is repeated for at most 10 steps. We do not introduce an additional verifier prompt for TTS; the same verifier prompt is reused to obtain the answer, explanation, and editing instruction. As shown in Table 8 and Fig. 6, verifier-guided refinement improves the relaxed score from 58.7 at the initial generation step to 63.5 after up to ten steps. Although the score does not monotonically increase at every intermediate step, the overall trend demonstrates that structured verification feedback can progressively correct scientific image generation errors. For reference, we also plug frontier MLLMs into the same loop as the critic. Gemini-3.5-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max reach 64.9 and 64.4 after ten steps, only 1.4 and 0.9 points above our 8B verifier, while Seed-2.0-Pro exhibits more volatile trajectory and ends at 62.6. This indicates that SciGen-Verifier delivers online-critic utility on par with much larger proprietary models at fraction of the inference cost. Note that this relaxed score is used only for the TTS application and is not directly comparable to the hierarchical Acca, Acce, and Acci metrics used in SciGen-Verify.

sections.content: E.1 ANNOTATION PROMPTS The following prompt templates summarize the AI-assisted annotation procedure for positive and negative examples in SciGen-Verify. Instance-specific variables such as {instruction} and {edit_explanation} are replaced for each example. Positive Explanation Annotation Prompt Role You are Senior Expert-Level Scientific Image Analyst. Your mission is to provide technical justification for the consistency between Generated Image and its Input Requirements. Objective The provided image and instruction are already consistent. Your task is to perform detailed visual-textual mapping to explain why they align, focusing on specific scientific evidence and visual markers within the image. Inputs Input Requirements (Ground Truth): {instruction} Visual Input: The last image provided in the conversation. Analysis Guidelines 1. Evidence-Based Mapping: Identify specific visual markers (e.g., data trends, chemical bonds, axis scales, or diagram components) that directly fulfill the requirements in the {instruction}. 2. Scientific Interpretation: Translate visual elements into technical confirmations (e.g., The downward slope of the curve confirms the negative correlation required). 3. No Redundancy: Do not simply repeat the instruction. Describe what is visually present that proves the instruction was followed. Mandatory Output Format Consistency Analysis. Provide concise, professional explanation that bridges the text requirements and the visual evidence. Format: Must be enclosed within <explanation> </explanation> tags. Requirement: Use bullet points for multiple markers to ensure scannability. Example <explanation> Consistency is confirmed through three key visual markers: 1. The molecular structure correctly displays the tetrahedral geometry at the chiral center as specified in the requirements. 2. The color-coding of the heat map strictly follows the viridis scale mentioned in the instruction, with the legend range correctly normalized from 0 to 1. 3. The X-axis correctly spans from 0 to 100 ms with the 10 ms interval markers explicitly rendered and aligned with the data points. </explanation> Modified-Instruction Negative Annotation Prompt Role You are Senior Expert-Level Scientific Image Auditor. Your task is to verify an existing image against newly updated instruction, using the provided modification rationale as your primary audit guide. Context Target Instruction: The new goal the image must satisfy. Modification Rationale: detailed explanation of what has changed and why the instruction was updated. Existing Image: The last image provided in the conversation, which was generated based on previous, now outdated version of the instruction. Audit Task 1. Analyze the Rationale: Identify the specific delta (changes) described in the Modification Rationale. 2. Verify Inconsistency: Inspect the Existing Image to find where it still follows the old logic and thus contradicts the Target Instruction. 3. Bridge the Gap: Determine what visual edits are necessary to align the image with the new requirements. Inputs Target Instruction: {instruction} Modification Rationale: {edit_explanation} Mandatory Output Format 1. Conflict Analysis. Identify precisely why the current image is now incorrect. Directly list visual elements that fail to meet the Target Instruction based on the Modification Rationale. Format: Must be enclosed within <explanation> </explanation> tags. Style: Concise, evidence-based, no filler words. 2. Actionable Editing Instruction. Provide step-by-step technical guide to transform the existing image into the target state. Format: Must be enclosed within <edit> </edit> tags. Requirement: Instructions must be concrete (e.g., Change the bar color from blue to green, Replace the legend label with B). Example <explanation> The Modification Rationale specifies shift from 2D plot to 3D perspective to show depth. The existing image remains 2D scatter plot, missing the Z-axis (Depth) and the corresponding data points required by the Target Instruction. </explanation> <edit> 1. Project the 2D scatter plot into 3D coordinate system. 2. Add Z-axis labeled Depth (nm). 3. Update the data points to include the third dimension values. </edit> 25 Code-Based Negative Annotation Prompt with Reference You are senior expert-level scientific image analysis model. There is misalignment between the requirements and the visual output. Compare the Image to be Fixed with the Correct Reference Image. Visual Input Image to be Fixed: The second to last image in the conversation. Correct Reference Image: The last image in the conversation. Input Requirements {instruction} Task & Output Format (Mandatory) 1. Conflict Analysis: Be extremely concise. Directly list the missing elements or visual discrepancies found in the Image to be Fixed when compared to the reference. This part MUST be enclosed within <explanation> </explanation> tags. 2. Actionable Editing Instruction: Provide targeted steps to correct the image. This part MUST be enclosed within <edit> </edit> tags. Example <explanation> The image is missing the error bars shown in the reference, the data trend is linear instead of polynomial, and the title font size is too small. </explanation> <edit> 1. Add vertical error bars to all data points. 2. Apply 2nd-order polynomial fit. 3. Increase title font size to 14pt. </edit> 26 Code-Based Negative Annotation Prompt without Reference You are senior expert-level scientific image analysis model. The generated image fails to satisfy the specified requirements. Visual Input The Existing Image is the last image in the conversation. Input Requirements {instruction} Task & Output Format (Mandatory) 1. Defect Analysis: Be extremely concise and critical. Directly list the elements from the instruction that are missing or incorrect in the image. Use format like None of the...: there is no X, no Y, and is wrong. This part MUST be enclosed within <explanation> </explanation> tags. 2. Actionable Editing Instruction: Provide clear instructions to repair the image. This part MUST be enclosed within <edit> </edit> tags. Example <explanation> None of the required annotations are present: there is no scale bar at the bottom right, no arrows pointing to the cell nucleus, and the stain color is blue instead of the required purple. </explanation> <edit> 1. Add 10µm scale bar to the bottom right. 2. Draw arrows pointing to the high-intensity regions. 3. Change the colormap to purple. </edit> E.2 VERIFIER INFERENCE PROMPT The following prompt is used for SciGen-Verifier inference and for baseline evaluation. The placeholder {instruction} is replaced by the task-specific scientific image generation or editing instruction, and the candidate image is attached at the <image> position. SciGen-Verifier Inference Prompt You are an expert scientific image verification model. Your task is to evaluate whether generated image correctly follows the given instruction. You must analyze the correctness of the generated image step by step, then provide final judgement. Task Types Instruction Following: Drawing/editing scientific diagrams based on explicit requirements (e.g., draw line at x=5, add axis labels, mark point P). Multidisciplinary Reasoning: Creating figures that require logical deduction (e.g., plotting calculated data points, geometric constructions based on given conditions). World Knowledge: Illustrating scientific concepts from domain knowledge (e.g., draw Earths internal layers, sketch plant cell structure). Instruction {instruction} Generated Image <image> Evaluation Rules 1. The instruction is the ONLY evaluation standard do not add requirements not mentioned in the instruction. 2. All equivalent implementations are correct (e.g., equivalent parallel circuits, either solid or dashed lines are acceptable if no style is specified). 3. Ignore all stylistic aspects unless explicitly required (e.g., colors, line thickness, font styles, marker shapes). 4. All explicitly requested elements must be present with correct values, positions, and labels. 5. The logical/scientific conclusion must be correct. Judgement true: All requirements fulfilled (equivalent implementations allowed), scientifically/logically correct. false: Any required element missing, any value/position wrong, or any scientific/logical error. Output <answer>true/false</answer> <explanation>Explain why the judgement is correct or incorrect.</explanation> <edit>If <answer> is false, provide concrete editing instructions to fix the image. If <answer> is true, do not output this tag.</edit> 28 E.

sections.title: JUDGE PROMPTS
sections.content: The following judge prompts are used to compute Acce and Acci. The explanation judge compares the predicted explanation with the ground-truth explanation, while the edit judge compares the predicted editing instruction with the ground-truth editing instruction. Explanation Evaluation Prompt You are strict evaluator for scientific image verification system. Your task is to compare the Predicted Explanation generated by model against the Ground Truth Explanation. Context (Instruction) {instruction} Ground Truth Judgement {gt_judgement} Ground Truth Explanation (Standard Answer) {gt_explanation} Predicted Explanation (To be Evaluated) {pred_explanation} Task Determine whether the Predicted Explanation captures the same verification rationale as the Ground Truth Explanation. For positive samples, it should identify the same key visual evidence supporting consistency with the instruction. For negative samples, it should identify the same core discrepancy, violated constraint, or scientific error. Judgement Criteria Return true if the predicted explanation captures the same key supporting evidence for positive sample, or the same core error for negative sample. Return false if the prediction is irrelevant, contradicts the instruction or ground truth, misses the main rationale, or introduces unsupported requirements. Output Format (JSON only) { "result": <boolean, true or false> } 29 Editing Instruction Evaluation Prompt You are senior scientific image editor. You are reviewing suggested Editing Instruction to fix an incorrect image based on Generation Context and the provided images. Background Context The Generation Context below includes the original instruction and the generated image result (represented by <image>). The generated image is incorrect and contains errors or deviations from the instruction requirements. Ground Truth Editing Instruction is provided as reference, which describes how to correctly fix the errors in the generated image. Generation Context (Instruction & Incorrect Image) {instruction} Incorrect Image: <image> Ground Truth Editing Instruction (Standard Reference for Fixing) {gt_edit} Predicted Editing Instruction (To be Evaluated) {pred_edit} Task Judge whether the Predicted Editing Instruction is valid and correct fix for the incorrect image. Compare it with the Ground Truth Editing Instruction and the visual context provided in the generation context. Return true if the predicted editing instruction is semantically consistent with the ground truth or effectively fixes the issue. Return false if the predicted editing instruction is irrelevant, incorrect, contradictory to the ground truth, or fails to address the core problem. Output Format (JSON only) { "result": <boolean, true or false> } 30 E.4 RUBRIC GENERATION PROMPT The following prompt is used to generate structured rubrics for SciGen-Rubric. The prompt requires each rubric to be valid JSON object with criteria, atomic yes/no checking points, and criterion scores summing to 10.0. Rubric Generation Prompt You are professional rubric generation expert. Your task is to generate precise, detailed scoring rubrics for evaluating AI-generated scientific diagrams. You will be given the original image generation instruction. Your output must be valid JSON object strictly following this format: { "rubric": [ { "criterion": "<The general evaluation criterion - high-level aspect to assess>", "points": ["<A specific yes/no sub-question>", . . . ], "score": <criterion_score> }, . . . ] } Rubric Structure Rules Total score across all criteria MUST sum to exactly 10.0 points. Allocate scores based on the number of distinct sub-requirements, points of failure, and structural importance. Criteria with more sub-elements or higher risk of visual error should receive proportionally higher scores. Criteria that are foundational or frequently violated should also receive higher scores. All score values must be rounded to 2 decimal places. Criterion Design Guidelines Each criterion should cover ONE distinct, non-overlapping evaluation dimension. Each point should be single, atomic, answerable yes/no question about that dimension. Points should cover: (1) presence/correctness of required elements, (2) absence of errors or unwanted extra elements, (3) structural/logical relationships. Questions must be answerable by visually inspecting the generated image against the original instruction. Use clear, specific language. Avoid vague terms like properly or adequately without definition. Important Only output the JSON object. Do NOT add any explanation, preamble, or additional text outside the JSON. The JSON must be parseable directly without any markdown formatting. 31 E.5 RUBRIC EVALUATION PROMPT The following prompt is used to semantically align candidate rubric rules with gold standard rules when computing RubricRecall, Non-HallucinationRate, and StructuralF1. The prompt enforces strict scope matching so that overly broad or vague candidate rules are not counted as valid hits. Rubric Semantic Matching Prompt You are an expert evaluator for the Rubric benchmark. Your task is to perform batch semantic alignment between set of Candidate Rubric Rules and set of Gold Standard Rules. Instruction Compare each Candidate Rule against the entire Gold Rules list. Determine if there is semantic match. Strict Matching Criteria Hit (YES) requires: 1. Specific Intent Match: The Candidate Rule must check the EXACT SAME constraint as the Gold Rule (e.g., if Gold checks Structure, Candidate must check Structure, not just Quality). 2. Scope Match: The Candidate Rule must not be significantly broader or vaguer than the Gold Rule. Automatic Rejection Criteria (NO) Vague vs Specific: If Candidate says Is the explanation good/detailed? and Gold says Does it mention Concept X?, this is NO. Different Dimension: If Candidate checks Content and Gold checks Structure/Formatting, this is NO. Partial Overlap: If Candidate checks Relevance but maps it to Gold Rule about Completeness, this is NO (unless the correct Gold Rule is missing). Evaluation Policy (Must Follow) Semantic equivalence means the Candidate Rule would accept and reject the same set of responses as the Gold Rule in practice. Any broadening, weakening, or generalization of constraints counts as scope mismatch. Do NOT combine partial overlaps across multiple Gold Rules to justify YES. If hit is NO, return an empty list for hit_gold_rule_indices. Critical JSON Rules 1. Wrap ALL keys and string values in double quotes. Never use single quotes. 2. Escape all literal double quotes inside strings using backslash, e.g., "Word". 3. Escape all newlines inside strings with n. Do not output literal line breaks inside strings. 4. Separate items in lists and dictionaries with commas. Do not miss the comma.
